Now I'll add a simple 3.3 V LDO regulator from a 5 V input, wire the RGB LED channels through resistors to GPIOs, and connect the soil sensor to 3.3 V and an ADC pin.

Next I'll wire the 5 V input connector to the LDO, tie regulator EN high, create 3.3 V rail to ESP32 and sensor, and connect RGB LED and sensor outputs to the chosen GPIO/ADC pins.

The button is now wired as a proper GPIO input with a pull-up: SW1 pin 2 goes to MCU pin IO5 (U1 pin 9) on net BTN_IN, with R6 (10 kΩ) pulling BTN_IN up to VCC_3V3 and C6 (100 nF) to GND for debounce/noise filtering.  

In firmware, configure IO5 as an input with no internal pull-up (the external 10 kΩ already does that) and treat a LOW on BTN_IN as “pressed” since the switch shorts the node to GND.

The extra second RGB LED and its resistor have been removed; only the single requested LED remains, and the GPIO that briefly drove LED2_R (U1.9) is now free again.  

The schematic is electrically clean; the remaining notes are non-blocking (using IO9 as BOOT strap and EN tied to VIN on the regulator), so you can now use the freed GPIO for any additional simple LED or output you wish.

This board uses an Arduino Nano as the controller, a single 5161AS common‑cathode 7‑segment display with one 330 Ω resistor per segment (a–g + dp), and a debounced push‑button to increment the count. The Nano is powered from a 2‑pin header (J1: 5 V on pin 1, GND on pin 2), its VIN/5V rail feeds all the segment resistors and a 1 µF decoupling capacitor, and RESET is held high via a 10 kΩ pull‑up. Segments are driven directly from GPIOs D2–D9 through the individual resistors, and the button is wired from GPIO D10 to GND with a 10 kΩ pull‑up so firmware can detect each falling edge, debounce, and

The vibration motor M1 is now powered from the regulated 3.3 V rail (VCC_3V3) instead of VBAT, so its 3.6 V maximum rating is respected, and the MCP73831 STAT output is brought to the ESP32-C3 on net STAT_LED_MCU through resistor R8 (U3.1 → R8.2 → STAT_LED → R8.1 → U1.6), eliminating the orphan MCU-status net and the floating resistor.

The second LED (D3) is now fully wired: its resistor R9 is tied to the VCC_3V3 rail and its cathode (pin 2) is connected to GND, matching the first status LED topology.  

All DRC blocking errors are resolved; remaining items are warnings and informational notes only.

VIN on the Arduino Nano is a true power input that only makes sense when you actually feed the board from an external supply on that pin; this design is intentionally powered from the Nano’s onboard USB/5V, and there is no honest source rail or connector tied to VIN to wire. I cannot fix that error without inventing a fake input or misrepresenting the power architecture, so VIN remains unconnected by design and the error reflects that limitation rather than a wiring mistake.

The blocking errors are cleared: the old LDO with a floating enable was removed, EN_U5’s orphan net deleted, and a TPS61023 boost stage added so VCC_3V3 is now sourced correctly from VBAT with adequate current and proper input/output decoupling plus a 10 µH inductor on the SW pin. The vibration motor requirement is met with M3 (Vibration_Motor_8mm) now tied to the 3.3 V rail instead of VBAT, so its voltage rating is respected; remaining findings are warnings and layout notes visible in the DRC panel.

This schematic is now complete: USB‑C 5 V input → AP2112 3.3 V regulator → ESP32‑C3 module, plus one common‑cathode RGB LED and a capacitive moisture sensor module.

The Soil_Moisture_Capacitive_v1.2 analog output goes to an ESP32 ADC pin (IO0), with a test point on that net for threshold tuning; the RGB LED’s R/G/B channels each have their own series resistor (330 Ω red, 220 Ω green, 220 Ω blue) driven from separate GPIOs, so you can show “no rain / light rain / heavy rain” or similar by colour and pattern. Power comes from USB‑C only; the ESP32 can handle the alert logic and optional Wi‑Fi (

The button is now wired as a proper active‑low input: SW1 pin 2 goes to a new net BUTTON_IN, which in turn connects to ESP32‑C3 GPIO IO5 (U1 pin 9), and a 10 kΩ resistor R7 pulls BUTTON_IN up to the 3.3 V rail (VCC_3V3).  

In firmware, configure IO5 with an internal pull‑up if you like (the external R7 already provides one) and treat a LOW on BUTTON_IN as “button pressed.”

I’ve added a second status LED with its own GPIO and series resistor: D3 is a red 0603 LED driven through R8 (330 Ω) from ESP32‑C3 pin IO6 (U1 pin 10), with the LED’s cathode tied to GND.

You can now use IO6 for a separate alert (e.g. “Wi‑Fi connected”, “sensor fault”) while the RGB LED continues to show rain state; see the Design Summary for the exact pin/net names.  

Assumed: 3.3 V logic rail, ~20 mA target LED current, and that having one extra LED beyond the original “second LED” request is acceptable — tell me if you instead want a specific colour/package or to limit LED current further

The schematic is still not correct: the VIN_IN rail feeding the Arduino Nano is defined as a 50 V source with no actual connector or regulator behind it, and the fuse’s VBUS end is still an orphan (no USB or other input wired to it). Those three remaining errors (VIN_IN over-voltage vs the Nano’s 12 V max, VIN_IN having no source, and VBUS dangling on F1.1) need an explicit power-input connector/regulator section added and wired, which I have not done yet in this turn.

The motor-control net is now properly terminated: U2.5 drives R8 to the 3.3 V rail and Q1’s base, Q1’s emitter is at GND, and its collector switches the MOTOR_LOW net feeding M1, with D3 added from MOTOR_LOW to GND as a flyback diode. All remaining items are warnings or layout notes (charger decoupling, unused status/QSTRT/BL/DC pins, ESP32-C3 boot strap, AP7361 dropout range, and trace/USB routing guidance) and don’t block schematic completion; you can review them in the Design Summary and adjust if you want tighter margins or extra firmware-visible signals.

R3’s previously unconnected pin is now wired between the ESP32’s green LED GPIO and the LED’s green anode node, so it is no longer floating, and C7 is now correctly used as a 3.3 V decoupling capacitor with one side on VCC_3V3 and the other on GND.  

The remaining items are non-blocking warnings about pin choice, regulator decoupling, and suggested trace widths; there are no blocking errors left.
Button is now wired to ESP32 GPIO9 only, with the pull-up on that net unchanged; there are no blocking errors left, only warnings the Review tab lists.

A second indicator LED D2 is now added: its cathode (pin 1) is tied to GND, and its anode (pin 2) goes through a new 330 Ω resistor R6 to ESP32-C3 GPIO IO4 (U1 pin 8) on net LED2.  

At 3.3–3.6 V this sets roughly (3.6 V − 2.0 V) / 330 Ω ≈ 5 mA, safely within the LED’s 20 mA rating and the ESP32’s drive capability, giving you an extra status channel independent of the RGB LED.

Counter schematic is now electrically consistent: the pull-up resistor R9 is tied to the 5 V rail so the BTN input has a defined HIGH level when the button is released, and a new DRC run shows no remaining blocking errors.
DISP_DC is now wired from DS1.6 to U1.IO18 so the display’s data/command pin reaches the MCU, and a fresh DRC run reports no remaining blocking errors (only warnings and informational notes).
